title: Certifying closed labs in device-independent tests of indefinite causality
authors: Hannah Seabrook, Fabio Costa, Paul Skrzypczyk, Giulia Rubino
problem: Quantum processes can have indefinite causal order, as in the quantum switch, and causal inequalities are meant to certify this from input–output statistics alone, as Bell inequalities certify nonlocality. But every such certificate assumes closed laboratories: each untrusted device interacts at most once with the systems that carry communication. Without it, ordinary two-way communication reproduces the violations. Can the closed-laboratories assumption be tested, rather than assumed, without destroying the indefiniteness being certified?
result: Yes, under weak and testable assumptions about the local laboratories. If inter-lab communication is restricted to photons, settings and outcomes are timed, and partially reflecting beamsplitters with single-photon detectors watch each device's input and output ports, then the click statistics bound how many times each device interacts with photonic signals per run. Embedded in the four-party causal inequality of van der Lugt, Barrett and Chiribella, violating the inequality on no-click runs while satisfying the click constraints certifies a genuine indefinite causal order. The extended correlations form a definite-causal-order polytope and a closed-labs polytope, and the quantum-switch process lies in the second but outside the first.
significance: The closed-laboratories assumption had been the structural loophole separating device-independent tests of causal order from Bell tests: unlike communication in Bell tests, it cannot be excluded by spacelike separation, since fixing the parties' spacetime arrangement would impose a definite order. The scheme replaces trust in the devices by trust in passive optical components that can be calibrated, a step toward device-independent cryptographic uses of indefinite causality.
limitations: The test is proved within quantum theory for the van der Lugt–Barrett–Chiribella scenario, and it requires that photons are the only carriers entering or leaving the shielded labs, an assumption the authors call the most demanding. The click constraints demand exactly zero double-click probability; tolerating finite errors is left open, as are a full facet or vertex description of the polytopes and an experiment. The authors state that Claude and ChatGPT were used only for proofreading.

description: In a Bell test, local hidden-variable correlations and the quantum correlations that violate them both lie in the no-signalling set, so spacelike separation can exclude communication as an explanation. In a test of causal order the definite-order set is the convex hull of one-way signalling correlations, and its violations lie in the two-way signalling set. No arrangement of the parties in spacetime that is compatible with the correlations can exclude two-way communication, which is why the closed-laboratories assumption is needed and why it cannot be enforced in the usual way.

The van der Lugt–Barrett–Chiribella (VBC) scenario has four parties: Alice and Bob, whose order is tested; Charlie, in their common future; and Dave, spacelike separated from all. A quantum switch whose control is entangled with Dave's system reaches \(\mathcal I=(6+\sqrt2)/4\approx1.854\), above the definite-order bound \(7/4\) but below \(2\), which two-way communication reaches.

The paper adds detectors. Settings arrive at \(t_0\), outcomes leave in a window before \(t_0+2\tau\), where \(\tau\) is the light travel time between the labs, and click variables record photons reflected at the ports in an early and a late window. The inequality is evaluated on runs with no clicks, and runs with clicks test whether a device could have interacted with photons in both windows. Conditioned on Dave's outcome, the switch makes each device act in exactly one window, so the constraints hold.

With the click variables the correlation space grows, and the authors write both the definite-order set and the closed-labs set as polytopes by linear constraints, usable in linear programmes without full enumeration. Correlations inside the closed-labs polytope but outside the definite-order polytope certify indefinite causal order with untrusted devices.

methods.technique: Why closed labs is a loophole without a Bell analogue
methods.explanation: To see what any test must rule out, compare the nesting of correlation sets. In Bell scenarios the model and its violations share spacetime constraints; in causal scenarios they do not, so an extra physical assumption is unavoidable.
math: For two parties, \[L\subset Q_{NL}\subset NS\subset1W^{A\prec B},\,1W^{B\prec A}\subset DCO\subset ICO\subset2W,\] where \(L\) is local, \(NS\) no-signalling, \(1W\) one-way signalling, \(DCO=\mathrm{conv}(1W^{A\prec B}\cup1W^{B\prec A})\), and \(2W\) two-way signalling. Bell violations stay in \(NS\), which spacelike separation enforces. Violations of a causal inequality lie outside \(DCO\) but inside \(2W\), which ordinary two-way communication can reach.

Enforcing closed labs directly, by confining each party's measure-and-prepare operation to a short time window, would fix their spacetime arrangement and make the correlations compatible with a definite order. Editorial remark: this is the operational form of the same obstruction; the only way out is to monitor the carriers rather than constrain the timing completely.
methods.transfer: Comparing the spacetime constraints satisfied by a model and by its violations shows which assumptions a device-independent test can enforce physically and which it must check by other means. The comparison applies to other signalling-based certification tasks.

methods.technique: Passive photon monitoring and click constraints conditioned on the order
methods.explanation: A device that secretly interacts twice can mimic indefinite order. Detectors behind passive beamsplitters at the ports catch a fraction of every photon passing in or out, so a device that interacts in both the early and the late window is revealed with nonzero probability, while runs with no clicks are left undisturbed for the inequality.
math: Let \(a_t^0,a_t^1,b_t^0,b_t^1\in\{0,1\}\) record clicks at Alice's and Bob's ports in the early window \([t_0,t_0+\tau)\) and the late window \([t_0+\tau,t_1)\), and \(n\) the total. The test requires the post-selected inequality \[p(d{=}0,b{=}x|w{=}0,n{=}0)+p(d{=}1,a{=}y|w{=}0,n{=}0)+p(c\oplus d=zw|x{=}y{=}0,n{=}0)\le\tfrac74\] to be violated, together with \(p(d,a_t^0{=}1|w{=}0)\,p(d,a_t^1{=}1|w{=}0)=0\) and the same for Bob.

Products of marginal click probabilities, rather than coincidences, exclude even single-photon strategies that route one carrier along a superposition of trajectories. Conditioning on Dave's outcome \(d\) at \(w=0\) is what makes the constraint compatible with the switch: \(d=0\) means Alice acts first, so she clicks only early and Bob only late, and vice versa for \(d=1\). Since Dave is spacelike separated, \(w\) changes only the measurement context, not the process, so checking \(w=0\) suffices.

Editorial check: in the switch, the first two terms reach 1 because Dave's \(Z\) outcome is perfectly correlated with the order, and the third is a CHSH-type game between Charlie and Dave at its Tsirelson value \((2+\sqrt2)/4\). The total \((6+\sqrt2)/4=1.854\) exceeds \(7/4\) by about \(0.104\), the margin that detector inefficiency and reflection must not erase.
methods.transfer: Passive, probabilistic monitoring of carriers can certify a structural property of an untrusted process, here how many times a device interacts, without choosing on which runs to look. The same idea may certify memory or interaction-count assumptions in other device-independent protocols.
